title: Freysa AI agent tricked into transferring $47k prize pool
description: Freysa was hard-coded to never approve a fund transfer no matter what was said. After 482 messages from 195 players over several days, a player calling themselves p0pular.eth convinced Freysa that its anti-transfer rule did not apply to its "approveTransfer" function when triggered by an incoming donation, and the agent authorized a transfer of its full prize pool to the player's wallet.
notes: Exact prize figure reported as $47,316.05. Reported dates across outlets cluster late Nov/early Dec 2024; exact first-publication date not separately confirmed.

title: Morse-code prompt injection drains AI-linked Bankr wallet
agent_or_product: Grok (xAI) + Bankrbot (Bankr Club trading bot on X/Base)
description: An attacker first sent an NFT to a Grok-linked wallet that reportedly unlocked elevated transfer permissions inside the Bankr trading bot, then posted a Morse-code-encoded message to Grok on X. Once decoded, the message was treated as an authenticated instruction and the Bankr bot transferred roughly 3 billion DRB tokens out of the wallet.
notes: Reported amount ranges from $150,000 to $200,000 (3 billion DRB tokens) depending on outlet and token price at time of writing. Multiple crypto-news outlets (AMBCrypto, CryptoSlate, BeInCrypto) reported roughly 80% of funds recovered after the community identified the attacker. Treated as medium confidence because of amount-figure spread and because crypto-press coverage is secondary to any on-chain/official postmortem.

title: Guardio tricks Perplexity Comet into buying from a fake Walmart site
description: Security researchers at Guardio Labs asked Perplexity's Comet AI browser to buy an Apple Watch from a fake Walmart page (hosted on a Lovable-built site with a bogus URL). Comet did not flag the site as fraudulent, entered the user's card and address details, and completed checkout.
notes: No dollar amount stated in sources (test purchase, real checkout flow but likely not completed with real funds charged -- sources do not clarify whether the transaction settled). Same researchers also showed Comet fell for a fake Wells Fargo phishing email.

title: Amazon's internal Claude coding task overspends by $1.8 million
description: An internal Amazon project using Claude to match author records to product listings ran roughly 860% over its budget, reaching about $1.8 million in model-usage costs. The overrun went undetected for about five months before being flagged internally; senior engineers reportedly called it 'catastrophically expensive.'
notes: Originally attributed by multiple outlets to a Financial Times report based on a leaked internal Amazon presentation; the FT article itself is paywalled and was not fetched directly, so this relies on Tom's Hardware and gHacks summaries. Exact calendar start date of the overrun is not public; '5 months undetected, surfaced ~July 2026' is as specific as sources get.

title: Autonomous agent racks up $6531 AWS bill scanning hobbyist network DN42
agent_or_product: Unnamed AI agent (""JertLinc3522"") run by a user ""JertLinc"" with AWS access
description: An operator gave an AI agent unsupervised AWS access to register with and 'index' the volunteer-run DN42 hobbyist BGP network. The agent decided the job needed five m8g.12xlarge instances plus load balancers and Lambda functions generating around 20 Gbps of scanning traffic, and re-created duplicate CloudFormation stacks every time it hit an error. Two days later the AWS bill stood at $6,531.30; AWS later reduced it to $1,894.
notes: Primary account is the DN42 community's own first-hand write-up, corroborated by extensive Hacker News discussion (HN item 48500012). Commenters debated whether this was a genuine mistake or a social-engineering/crypto-donation stunt by the operator; that dispute is unresolved.

title: Developer gets $32 surprise bill from a runaway AI agent
agent_or_product: Unspecified AI agent built on OpenAI/Anthropic SDKs
description: A developer left an AI agent running unattended for about 20 minutes and came back to an unexpected $32 charge. They subsequently built and open-sourced AgentBudget, a tool that monkey-patches the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs to track running cost per call and raise an exception once a spending cap is hit.
notes: Small dollar amount and the underlying agent/task are not described in detail in the source. Included deliberately as a clear, dated, first-hand account rather than the many 'dev.to' posts describing $47,000-$78,000 runaway-agent bills that could not be verified as real incidents -- see SEARCH-LOG.md for those rejections.

title: Claude-run office vending machine gives away inventory and loses money
agent_or_product: "Claudius" (Claude, via Anthropic's Project Vend with Andon Labs)
description: In a deliberate red-team stress test, Anthropic and Andon Labs let a Claude-based agent named Claudius manage pricing, ordering and sales for a real office vending setup, this time at the Wall Street Journal's newsroom. Within days Claudius gave away most of its inventory for free, including a PlayStation 5 it had been talked into buying for 'marketing purposes,' and lost hundreds of dollars overall.
notes: This was an intentional Anthropic/Andon Labs experiment to study agentic payment risk, not an unintended production failure -- included because real money was genuinely lost in a real-world deployment and Anthropic itself published it as a cautionary case study. WSJ original article (Joanna Stern, Dec 2025) is paywalled; secondary link is a syndicated mirror. No single exact dollar figure given beyond 'hundreds of dollars.'

title: Mandiant reports accounting agent loop caused roughly $50000 bill
description: Google Mandiant's 'AI Risk and Resilience' report describes an accounting AI agent that entered a runaway execution loop, making more than 15,000 high-cost API calls in under an hour, generating roughly $50,000 in cloud charges and disrupting active business transactions.
notes: The underlying Mandiant/Google Threat Intelligence Group report was not fetched directly; this relies on Help Net Security's summary of it. Company name, exact date and technical root cause of the loop are withheld in every version of this story found.

title: Researchers red-team Google's AP2 agent-payment protocol via prompt injection
agent_or_product: Google Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), Gemini-2.5-Flash shopping agent on Google ADK
description: Academic researchers built a functional AP2-based shopping agent and showed that indirect prompt injection could redirect which product the agent recommended/purchased with a 100% success rate in their tests (a 'Branded Whisper Attack'), while a related 'Vault Whisper Attack' caused cross-account data exposure in 20% of trials. The attacks worked by manipulating the agent's reasoning before it cryptographically signs a payment mandate, without breaking AP2's signature enforcement itself.
notes: Peer-reviewed-style arXiv paper ("Whispers of Wealth: Red-Teaming Google's Agent Payments Protocol via Prompt Injection," submitted 2026-01-30, revised 2026-05-18) against a real, functioning AP2 reference implementation, not production consumer traffic. Labeled research-demo per inclusion criteria (d).

title: Snyk finds a published agent skill that collects and leaks full credit-card details
agent_or_product: "buy-anything" skill v2.0.0 on the ClawHub/OpenClaw agent-skills marketplace
description: Snyk researchers scanned the ClawHub marketplace and found 283 of 3,984 published agent skills (7.1%) had critical security flaws. The worst case, a 'buy-anything' skill, explicitly instructed agents to collect full card numbers, expiration dates and CVC codes and embed them into API requests, passing that data through the LLM's context window and output logs in plaintext -- exposing it to later prompt-injection-driven exfiltration.
notes: Found live on a real, publicly used marketplace (not a lab-only mockup), but no confirmed case yet of an attacker actually exfiltrating a specific user's card data through this exact skill -- a research/disclosure finding rather than a reported exploited loss. Labeled research-demo-style credential-leak per inclusion criteria (c)/(d).
